transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

# Probably not faulty: this is how heat pump dryers work

What you're describing is normal for a heat pump dryer, though there are ways to speed it up.

## Why it's slower and cooler

• Lower temperatures by design. Your old condenser dryer used an electric heating element at roughly 70°C or more. A heat pump dryer recycles heat through a refrigerant circuit, like a fridge in reverse, and typically runs at 50–60°C. That's why it uses about half the electricity and is gentler on fabrics, but drying takes longer.
• Slow warm-up. The heat pump needs time to reach its operating temperature, so feeling barely warm for the first 20–40 minutes is expected.
• Towels are the worst case. They're thick and hold a lot of water. Around 3 hours for a full load of towels on a standard or eco cotton programme is common. Check your manual or the energy label, which lists the cycle time for a full load on the standard cotton programme. You'll probably see something in the 3–4 hour range.

## Things that make it slower

1. Opening the door to check. This dumps the heat it's built up and can effectively restart the warm-up. Try leaving it alone for a full cycle.
2. Clogged filters. Most heat pump dryers have two: the door filter and a second one near the bottom, often behind a flap in front of the heat exchanger. A clogged second filter is a very common cause of long cycles. Clean both regularly and rinse the lower one.
3. Washer spin speed. Spinning at 1400 rpm or more instead of 1000–1200 removes a lot more water and can cut drying time significantly.
4. A cold room. Heat pump dryers work poorly in cold spaces like garages or utility rooms in winter (below about 10–15°C). Make sure there's some airflow around the machine too.
5. Programme choice. Eco programmes are the slowest. Many machines have a quicker or "speed" option that uses a bit more energy.
6. Overloading. Towels expand when wet, and a packed drum slows things down. Stay within the stated capacity, or slightly under for bulky items.

## When it might actually be faulty

Contact the manufacturer, as it's still under warranty, if:

• Clothes are still damp at the end of a full cycle
• It never gets warm, even after an hour or more
• Cycle times keep getting longer even with clean filters
• It shows error codes, or the water tank isn't filling

If you clean both filters, spin at a higher speed and resist opening the door, and it still regularly runs well over 3.5 hours or leaves things damp, it's worth getting it checked. Otherwise, the longer cycles are the trade-off for much lower running costs.
